title: Continuity with the epsilons hidden

prereqs.why: This is one direction of the theorem that replaces epsilons and deltas by open sets.
The epsilon-delta definition is the hypothesis, and it is used once.
That a point of an open set has a ball about it inside the set is used twice, once at each end.

statement:
**Theorem.** Let $f : X \to Y$ be a map between metric spaces. If $f$ is
continuous at every point of $X$, then $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$ for every
open $V \subseteq Y$.

The proof below is complete except for the reasons. Choose the
justification for each marked step.

Throughout, $f^{-1}(V) = \{\,x \in X : f(x) \in V\,\}$. No assumption is made
that $f$ is injective, surjective or anything else: $f^{-1}$ here is the
preimage of a set, not an inverse function.
hints: To show a set is open you take an arbitrary point of it and produce a ball about that point inside the set. Write down what that means here before reading on.
You have two open-set facts available and one continuity fact. The open-set fact about $V$ gives you an $\eps$; continuity turns that $\eps$ into a $\delta$.
The last step is pure set theory: $f(x) \in V$ is the definition of $x \in f^{-1}(V)$, and nothing metric is used.

payload.claim: **Theorem.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous at every point, then the preimage of every open set is open.

steps.text: Let $V \subseteq Y$ be open and let $a \in f^{-1}(V)$. We must produce $r > 0$ with $B(a, r) \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$.
$f(a) \in V$, so there is $\eps > 0$ with $B\bigl(f(a), \eps\bigr) \subseteq V$.
There is $\delta > 0$ such that $d_X(x, a) < \delta$ implies $d_Y\bigl(f(x), f(a)\bigr) < \eps$.
Hence $f(x) \in V$, which is to say $x \in f^{-1}(V)$.
So $B(a,\delta) \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$. As $a$ was an arbitrary point of $f^{-1}(V)$, that set is open. $\blacksquare$

choices: $V$ is open, and every point of an open set has a ball about it inside the set
the definitions of the two balls, applied to the implication just quoted
the choice of $\eps$ in the second step, which put $B(f(a),\eps)$ inside $V$
$f$ is injective, so preimages and images agree
the preimage of a closed set is closed
